headings.title: Introduction to the Chi-Square Test
headings.content: The Chi-Square test is a fundamental non-parametric statistical method widely utilized in nursing and healthcare research to analyze categorical data. Unlike parametric tests such as the t-test or ANOVA, which require continuous data and normally distributed populations, the Chi-Square test evaluates proportions, counts, and frequencies. In nursing studies, researchers frequently encounter categorical variables, such as patient gender, smoking status, types of wound care products, compliance categories, or disease stages. The primary purpose of the Chi-Square test is to determine whether there is a statistically significant association between two or more categorical variables, or whether an observed distribution of data significantly differs from a theoretically expected distribution. For instance, a nursing researcher might use a Chi-Square test to investigate whether there is an association between the incidence of pressure ulcers and the type of mattress used in a medical-surgical ward. Because healthcare data is often measured on nominal or ordinal scales, mastering the Chi-Square test is essential for nursing students preparing for board examinations and evidence-based practice modules. It allows clinicians to interpret cross-tabulation tables, commonly known as contingency tables, and make data-driven decisions regarding patient care outcomes, safety protocols, and public health interventions.

headings.title: Underlying Assumptions and Requirements
headings.content: To ensure the validity and reliability of the results obtained from a Chi-Square test, several underlying statistical assumptions and requirements must be met. First, the data must be in the form of frequencies or counts of cases, rather than percentages, raw scores, or transformed data. Second, the variables involved must be categorical, measured on a nominal or ordinal scale. Third, the observations must be independent of one another. This means that each study participant or subject can only contribute data to one cell within a contingency table; a single patient's responses cannot be counted multiple times across different categories. Fourth, a crucial sample size requirement dictates that the expected frequency in any single cell of the contingency table should not be too small. Standard statistical convention dictates that at least 80% of the cells must have an expected frequency of 5 or greater, and no cell should have an expected frequency of less than 1. If this assumption is violated, particularly in small sample sizes within clinical trials, alternative tests such as Fisher's Exact Test must be utilized instead. Nursing researchers must carefully verify these assumptions before computing the test statistic to avoid Type I or Type II errors in clinical studies.

headings.title: Types of Chi-Square Tests: Goodness-of-Fit vs. Test of Independence
headings.content: In nursing and health sciences research, Chi-Square analysis is generally divided into two distinct types: the Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test and the Chi-Square Test of Independence. The Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test is a single-variable test used to determine whether a sample of categorical data matches a known or hypothesized theoretical population distribution. For example, a nurse manager might use this test to see if the distribution of blood types among patients admitted to an emergency department matches the known national blood type distribution. In contrast, the Chi-Square Test of Independence involves two categorical variables and evaluates whether an association exists between them. This is the most common application in nursing research. It uses a contingency table to cross-classify subjects based on both variables simultaneously. An example would be testing whether patient satisfaction levels (satisfied vs. unsatisfied) are independent of the shift during which care was delivered (morning, afternoon, night). Understanding the distinction between these two tests helps nursing students correctly set up their research questions, choose appropriate software commands, and accurately interpret their findings in clinical audits or quality improvement projects.

headings.title: Formulating Hypotheses for Chi-Square Analysis
headings.content: Formulating clear null and alternative hypotheses is a mandatory step before conducting any Chi-Square analysis in nursing research. The null hypothesis (H₀) generally states that there is no relationship, no association, or no difference between the categorical variables being studied. In the context of a Test of Independence, H₀ asserts that the two variables are independent of one another. Conversely, the alternative hypothesis (H₁) posits that a significant relationship, association, or difference does exist between the variables, meaning they are dependent. For example, if a nurse researcher is investigating the relationship between patient fall rates and the implementation of a new bed-alarm system, the hypotheses would be structured as follows: H₀: Patient fall rates and the use of bed-alarm systems are independent (no association), and H₁: Patient fall rates and the use of bed-alarm systems are dependent (an association exists). Establishing these hypotheses prior to data analysis prevents confirmation bias and guides the evaluation of the p-value against the chosen significance level (alpha), which is typically set at 0.05 in nursing literature.

headings.title: Calculating Expected and Observed Frequencies
headings.content: The core computation of the Chi-Square statistic relies on comparing the observed frequencies (O) that researchers actually find in their sample data with the expected frequencies (E) that would be expected if the null hypothesis were entirely true. Observed frequencies are the direct counts recorded during data collection and placed into the cells of a contingency table. Expected frequencies, on the other hand, are calculated mathematically for each cell using the formula: E = (Row Total × Column Total) / Grand Total. Once both observed and expected frequencies are established, the Chi-Square test statistic formula is applied: χ² = Σ [ (O - E)² / E ], where the sum is taken across all cells in the table. This formula calculates the squared difference between what was observed and what was expected, standardizes it by dividing by the expected frequency, and sums these values up. A larger overall Chi-Square value indicates a greater divergence between the observed data and the expected model, suggesting that the null hypothesis is unlikely to be true. Nursing students must understand this arithmetic logic because statistical software packages like SPSS or R perform these exact calculations behind the scenes, and clinicians should know how the underlying metrics are derived.

headings.title: Interpreting Chi-Square Test Results and P-Values
headings.content: Once the Chi-Square test statistic is calculated, the next vital step is interpreting the results using degrees of freedom (df) and the resulting p-value. The degrees of freedom for a Chi-Square test of independence are calculated as df = (r - 1) × (c - 1), where 'r' is the number of rows and 'c' is the number of columns in the contingency table. By referencing the calculated Chi-Square value and the degrees of freedom against a standard Chi-Square distribution table, or by letting statistical software compute it, a p-value is generated. In evidence-based nursing practice, a significance level (alpha) of 0.05 is standard. If the resulting p-value is less than or equal to 0.05 (p ≤ 0.05), the researcher rejects the null hypothesis, concluding that the association between the categorical variables is statistically significant. Conversely, if the p-value is greater than 0.05 (p > 0.05), the researcher fails to reject the null hypothesis, indicating insufficient evidence to claim an association. It is important for nursing professionals to remember that statistical significance does not automatically equate to clinical significance; a finding might be statistically significant due to a very large sample size, yet have minimal impact on actual patient care outcomes.

headings.title: Application and Reporting in Nursing Research
headings.content: Effectively applying and reporting Chi-Square test results in nursing research and scholarly writing requires adherence to standardized reporting formats, such as those recommended by the American Psychological Association (APA) guidelines. When reporting Chi-Square findings in a nursing journal or research project, the text must include the degrees of freedom, the sample size or total count, the calculated test statistic value rounded to two decimal places, and the exact p-value. A standard reporting template looks like this: χ²(df, N = total) = value, p = value. For example, a nurse researcher might write: 'A significant association was found between patient adherence to medication regimens and their level of health literacy, χ²(2, N = 150) = 8.45, p = .015.' In addition to numerical reporting, findings should be summarized using clear contingency tables or bar charts to help clinical readers visualize the proportional differences between groups. Furthermore, nursing discussions must contextualize these statistical results by explaining their practical implications for patient education, nursing interventions, and healthcare policy, bridging the gap between raw statistical output and improved bedside nursing care.
